title: Nehemiah 13:23–31
context: Nehemiah finds Jews married to women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, whose children cannot speak the Jews’ language; he confronts them harshly and makes them swear not to arrange such marriages, recalling that foreign wives led even Solomon to sin. A grandson of Eliashib the high priest is son-in-law to Sanballat, and Nehemiah drives him away and prays against those who defiled the priesthood, then appoints the duties of priests and Levites. Both traditions read the concern as covenant faithfulness and worship rather than ethnicity as such, and they describe Nehemiah’s actions as the text reports them without presenting them as a model.

verses.text: In those days I also saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab;
verses.arminianNotes:
“In those days I also saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab.” Arminian readers note that this repeats a problem addressed earlier (Ezra 9–10) and broke the pledge of 10:30.

The narrative reports a recurring struggle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the community again drifting from its covenant commitments.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the passage soberly, recognizing the real people and families involved.

verses.text: and their children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews’ language, but according to the language of each people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah reports that “their children spoke half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews” language.’ Arminian readers note the concern that children could not take part in the community’s life and worship.

The law had been read and explained in that language (8:8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a concern for passing on covenant faith to the next generation.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the issue the text raises is the children’s ability to share in the life of God’s people.

verses.text: I contended with them, cursed them, struck certain of them, plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God, “You shall not give your daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for your sons, or for yourselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah “contended with them, cursed them, struck certain of them, plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God.” Arminian readers note that the text reports these harsh actions plainly.

Ezra had pulled out his own hair in grief (Ezra 9:3); Nehemiah acts against others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read the account as narrative and do not present it as a model for discipline today.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the oath concerns future marriages, and the passage records Nehemiah’s zeal without endorsing every action.

verses.text: Didn’t Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? Yet among many nations there was no king like him, and he was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Nevertheless foreign women caused even him to sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Didn’t Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?... Nevertheless foreign women caused even him to sin.” Arminian readers note that the concern is turning away from God, as with Solomon (1 Kings 11:1–4).

The danger is idolatry, not ethnicity as such.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see covenant faithfulness and worship at stake (cf. Deut 7:3–4).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Solomon was “loved by his God,” yet his marriages led his heart astray, which is the warning Nehemiah draws.

verses.text: Shall we then listen to you to do all this great evil, to trespass against our God in marrying foreign women?”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Shall we then listen to you to do all this great evil, to trespass against our God in marrying foreign women?” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah frames the issue as trespass against God.

The concern is faithfulness to the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same focus on the people’s relationship with God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both note that Scripture also honors foreigners who joined Israel in faith, such as Rahab and Ruth (cf. Matt 1:5).

verses.text: One of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite; therefore I chased him from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“One of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite; therefore I chased him from me.” Arminian readers note that the high priest’s family had allied with Nehemiah’s opponent (2:10).

The text reports his removal briefly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a particular concern for the purity of the priesthood (cf. Lev 21:14).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the verse soberly, without speculating about the man beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Remember them, my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Remember them, my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah commits judgment to God.

The covenant with the priests is recalled (cf. Num 25:12–13; Mal 2:4–8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prayer entrusting the matter to God.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Nehemiah’s concern is the faithfulness of those who lead worship.

verses.text: Thus I cleansed them from all foreigners and appointed duties for the priests and for the Levites, everyone in his work;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Thus I cleansed them from all foreigners and appointed duties for the priests and for the Levites, everyone in his work.” Arminian readers note that the reform ends with ordered service restored.

The text summarizes the actions briefly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the priesthood set again to its proper work.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the verse as Nehemiah’s report, not as a model for how communities should treat outsiders.

verses.text: and for the wood offering, at appointed times, and for the first fruits. Remember me, my God, for good.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah appoints the wood offering and the first fruits (cf. 10:34–35), and prays, “Remember me, my God, for good.” Arminian readers note that the book ends with a prayer.

Nehemiah entrusts his work to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the final prayer as an appeal to God’s goodness.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the book closes with practical faithfulness and a prayer for God’s remembrance, leaving the outcome in his hands.
